reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: An acquired bleeding disorder caused by autoantibodies (inhibitors) that neutralise a clotting factor, most commonly factor VIII
Unlike congenital haemophilia, it arises in previously unaffected individuals, typically older adults, and lacks a lifelong or family bleeding history
The bleeding pattern differs from inherited haemophilia: extensive soft-tissue and mucosal bleeding, spontaneous bruising and haematomas are common, while haemarthroses are relatively infrequent
It is often idiopathic but may be associated with pregnancy and the postpartum period, autoimmune disease, malignancy, and certain drugs
The characteristic laboratory picture is an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) with a normal prothrombin time and platelet count
A mixing study fails to correct the APTT (and worsens on incubation), pointing to an inhibitor rather than a factor deficiency
Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating a reduced factor VIII level with a measurable inhibitor titre (Bethesda assay)
Management has two aims: controlling acute bleeding with agents that bypass factor VIII, and eradicating the inhibitor with immunosuppression
Prompt haematology involvement is essential because bleeding can be sudden, severe and life-threatening
reference.pathophysiology: Acquired haemophilia results from the spontaneous development of autoantibodies directed against a coagulation factor, most often factor VIII. These inhibitory antibodies bind and neutralise the factor, impairing the intrinsic coagulation pathway and clot formation. In contrast to the alloantibodies seen in congenital haemophilia, these autoantibodies show complex (non-linear) inhibition kinetics, so residual factor activity may be detectable yet bleeding is still severe. The trigger for autoantibody formation is frequently unknown, but recognised associations include the postpartum state, autoimmune disorders, underlying malignancy and drug reactions, all reflecting dysregulated immune tolerance.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital haemophilia with an alloantibody inhibitor
Acquired or inherited von Willebrand disease
Lupus anticoagulant (prolongs APTT but is typically thrombotic, not bleeding)
Other clotting factor inhibitors or deficiencies
additionalInvestigations: Coagulation screen showing isolated prolonged APTT with normal PT
Mixing study with immediate and incubated samples to detect a time-dependent inhibitor
Bethesda assay to quantify the inhibitor titre
Investigation for underlying associations: autoimmune screen, age-appropriate malignancy evaluation and pregnancy history
redFlags: Acute major or life-threatening bleeding (retroperitoneal, gastrointestinal, intracranial or airway)
Extensive spontaneous soft-tissue haematomas with rapidly falling haemoglobin
New unexplained bleeding with an isolated prolonged APTT in an older or postpartum patient
Bleeding not responding to standard factor replacement, indicating an inhibitor
reference.prognosis: Acquired haemophilia carries significant morbidity and mortality from severe bleeding, particularly at presentation, but with prompt haemostatic control and immunosuppressive inhibitor eradication many patients achieve durable remission. Prognosis is influenced by the severity of bleeding, the inhibitor titre, the patient's age and comorbidities, and any underlying disorder such as malignancy.
pitfalls: Attributing an isolated prolonged APTT to an artefact or anticoagulant and missing the inhibitor
Assuming standard factor VIII replacement will control bleeding, when bypassing agents are usually required
Delaying immunosuppression to eradicate the inhibitor
Failing to search for an underlying malignancy or autoimmune trigger
Undertaking invasive procedures without recognising the profound bleeding risk
